q: What happens to guard cells when water enters them?
exp: Stomata are small pores on the leaf epidermis that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Turgid guard cells open the pore, while water loss makes guard cells relaxed or shrunken and closes it.

q: What happens to the stoma when guard cells become turgid?
exp: Stomata are small pores on the leaf epidermis that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Turgid guard cells open the pore, while water loss makes guard cells relaxed or shrunken and closes it.

q: What happens to guard cells when water exits them?
a: They become loose, relaxed or shrunken.
exp: Stomata are small pores on the leaf epidermis that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Turgid guard cells open the pore, while water loss makes guard cells relaxed or shrunken and closes it.

q: What happens to the stoma when guard cells lose water?
exp: Stomata are small pores on the leaf epidermis that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Turgid guard cells open the pore, while water loss makes guard cells relaxed or shrunken and closes it.

q: When does a stoma open?
a: When water enters guard cells and they become turgid.
exp: Stomata are small pores on the leaf epidermis that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Turgid guard cells open the pore, while water loss makes guard cells relaxed or shrunken and closes it.

q: When does a stoma close?
a: When water exits guard cells and they become relaxed or shrunken.
exp: Stomata are small pores on the leaf epidermis that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Turgid guard cells open the pore, while water loss makes guard cells relaxed or shrunken and closes it.

q: Which comparison of guard-cell shape is most accurate?
a: Many dicots have kidney-shaped guard cells, whereas grasses have dumbbell-shaped guard cells.
exp: NCERT highlights bean/kidney-shaped guard cells in many plants and dumbbell-shaped guard cells in grasses. 'Monocot = dumbbell' is too broad as a universal statement.

q: What is the chief function of epithelial tissue?
exp: Epithelial tissue mainly provides protection and lining. Its cells are arranged continuously and densely over body surfaces, organs and cavities of organ systems.

q: What does epithelial tissue primarily cover or line?
a: Body surfaces and the linings of internal cavities, ducts and tubes.
exp: Epithelia form protective coverings and internal linings and also contribute to glands. Their cells are closely packed with little intercellular matrix.

q: How are epithelial cells arranged?
exp: Epithelial tissue mainly provides protection and lining. Its cells are arranged continuously and densely over body surfaces, organs and cavities of organ systems.

q: How is simple squamous epithelium described?
exp: Simple squamous epithelium is a thin, flat, single layer. It is found in blood vessels, alveoli, the mouth and alimentary canal.

q: Which pair is a typical site of simple squamous epithelium?
a: Alveoli of lungs and lining of blood vessels
exp: Simple squamous epithelium is thin and suited for diffusion or filtration, as in lung alveoli and vascular endothelium.

q: How is stratified squamous epithelium described?
exp: Stratified squamous epithelium is multilayered and is the epithelial type associated with skin.

q: Where is stratified squamous epithelium typically found?
a: In the epidermis of skin and in non-keratinised form in regions such as the mouth and oesophagus.
exp: Stratification protects against abrasion. Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium occurs in skin; non-keratinised forms line moist surfaces such as mouth and oesophagus.

q: How is cuboidal epithelium described?
exp: Cuboidal epithelium is made of cube-shaped cells. It is associated with kidney tubules, sweat glands, salivary glands and thyroid glands.

q: Which sites commonly contain simple cuboidal epithelium?
a: Kidney tubules and ducts of many glands; thyroid follicles are another example.
exp: Cuboidal epithelium is suited to secretion and absorption and is classically found in kidney tubules and glandular ducts.

q: How is columnar epithelium described?
exp: Columnar epithelium has column-shaped cells and is associated with the stomach, intestine, gall bladder and bile duct.

q: Where is simple columnar epithelium commonly found?
a: Along much of the stomach and intestinal lining; the gallbladder is another example.
exp: Simple columnar epithelium performs absorption and secretion in the digestive tract and also lines the gallbladder.

q: How is ciliated columnar epithelium described?
a: Hair-like cilia on the free surface.
exp: Ciliated columnar epithelium bears motile cilia on its free surface. Standard examples include respiratory passages such as the trachea and the oviduct; the cilia move mucus or reproductive material along the surface.

q: Which pair is a standard site of ciliated columnar epithelium?
a: Respiratory passages such as the trachea and the oviducts
exp: Cilia in respiratory epithelium move mucus and trapped particles, while cilia in the oviduct help move the ovum/early embryo. Vas deferens is not the standard NCERT example for motile ciliated columnar epithelium.

q: Which epithelium is found in blood vessels?
exp: Blood is a connective tissue that transports nutrients, oxygen/carbon dioxide, hormones and excretory materials. About 55% is plasma and 45% is cells.

q: Which epithelium is found in alveoli?
exp: Simple squamous epithelium is a thin, flat, single layer. It is found in blood vessels, alveoli, the mouth and alimentary canal.

q: Which epithelium is found in skin?
exp: Stratified squamous epithelium is multilayered and is the epithelial type associated with skin.

q: Which epithelium is found in kidney tubules?
exp: Cuboidal epithelium is made of cube-shaped cells. It is associated with kidney tubules, sweat glands, salivary glands and thyroid glands.

q: Which epithelium is found in sweat glands?
exp: Cuboidal epithelium is made of cube-shaped cells. It is associated with kidney tubules, sweat glands, salivary glands and thyroid glands.

q: Which epithelium is found in salivary glands?
exp: Cuboidal epithelium is made of cube-shaped cells. It is associated with kidney tubules, sweat glands, salivary glands and thyroid glands.

q: Which epithelium is found in thyroid glands?
exp: Cuboidal epithelium is made of cube-shaped cells. It is associated with kidney tubules, sweat glands, salivary glands and thyroid glands.

q: Which epithelium is found in the stomach and intestine?
exp: Columnar epithelium has column-shaped cells and is associated with the stomach, intestine, gall bladder and bile duct.

q: Which epithelium lines the gallbladder?
exp: The gallbladder is lined by simple columnar epithelium specialised mainly for absorption and secretion.

q: Which epithelium is found in the trachea?
exp: Ciliated columnar epithelium bears motile cilia on its free surface. Standard examples include respiratory passages such as the trachea and the oviduct; the cilia move mucus or reproductive material along the surface.

q: Which epithelium is found in the oviduct?
exp: Ciliated columnar epithelium bears motile cilia on its free surface. Standard examples include respiratory passages such as the trachea and the oviduct; the cilia move mucus or reproductive material along the surface.

q: What is an important function of cilia in the oviduct?
a: To help move the ovum and early embryo toward the uterus.
exp: Coordinated ciliary beating in the oviduct contributes to transport of the ovum/early embryo toward the uterus.

q: What special structure is present on ciliated columnar epithelium?
a: Hair-like cilia on the free surface.
exp: Ciliated columnar epithelium bears motile cilia on its free surface. Standard examples include respiratory passages such as the trachea and the oviduct; the cilia move mucus or reproductive material along the surface.

q: What is a goblet cell in this classification?
exp: A goblet cell represents single-cell glandular epithelium, while glands are the multicellular form. Salivary and thyroid glands are the examples paired with the multicellular form.

q: What is the multicellular form of glandular epithelium?
exp: A goblet cell represents single-cell glandular epithelium, while glands are the multicellular form. Salivary and thyroid glands are the examples paired with the multicellular form.

q: Which are examples of multicellular glands?
exp: A goblet cell represents single-cell glandular epithelium, while glands are the multicellular form. Salivary and thyroid glands are the examples paired with the multicellular form.

q: What memory code is given for simple epithelial types?
a: Squamous, Cuboidal, Columnar, Ciliated columnar -> SC3.
exp: The memory code SC3 groups the simple epithelial types as Squamous, Cuboidal, Columnar and Ciliated columnar.

q: Which statement correctly describes the epithelium of skin?
exp: Stratified squamous epithelium is multilayered and is the epithelial type associated with skin.

q: Which statement correctly describes the epithelium of kidney tubules?
exp: Cuboidal epithelium is made of cube-shaped cells. It is associated with kidney tubules, sweat glands, salivary glands and thyroid glands.

q: Which statement correctly describes the epithelium of the trachea?
exp: Ciliated columnar epithelium bears motile cilia on its free surface. Standard examples include respiratory passages such as the trachea and the oviduct; the cilia move mucus or reproductive material along the surface.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What is the main role of connective tissue?
a: Connecting different organs and body parts.
exp: Connective tissue connects different organs and body parts. Its cells are embedded in an intercellular matrix, and the group includes fibrous, fluid, loose and skeletal connective tissues.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Where are connective-tissue cells embedded?
exp: Connective tissue connects different organs and body parts. Its cells are embedded in an intercellular matrix, and the group includes fibrous, fluid, loose and skeletal connective tissues.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What does a tendon connect?
exp: Tendons are dense regular connective tissues that transmit force from skeletal muscle to bone.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What is the predominant fibre in a tendon?
a: Collagen fibres arranged in dense parallel bundles
exp: Tendons are collagen-rich and the fibres are aligned with the direction of pull, giving high tensile strength.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: How does a tendon compare with a ligament mechanically?
a: A tendon is very strong and relatively less elastic.
exp: Tendon collagen bundles provide high tensile strength with relatively limited stretch compared with many ligaments.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What does a ligament connect?
exp: Ligaments connect bone to bone at joints. They are collagen-rich and are generally more elastic than tendons because many contain a relatively greater elastic-fibre component; they are not made of elastin alone.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which statement about fibres in ligaments is most accurate?
a: Ligaments are collagen-rich and generally contain a greater elastic-fibre component than tendons.
exp: Both tendons and ligaments contain abundant collagen. Many ligaments are more elastic than tendons because they have relatively more elastic fibres, but 'ligament = elastin only' is incorrect.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which property is generally greater in a ligament than in a tendon?
exp: Ligaments connect bones at joints and must permit controlled movement, so they are generally more flexible and elastic than tendons.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which connective tissue connects bone to muscle?
exp: Bone is hard and stiff because its matrix contains calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate salts. Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells, and bone provides support, protection and body shape.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which connective tissue connects bone to bone?
exp: Bone is hard and stiff because its matrix contains calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate salts. Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells, and bone provides support, protection and body shape.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which has white collagen filaments: tendon or ligament?
exp: Tendon connects bone to muscle and contains white collagen filaments. It is strong but has limited flexibility.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Compared with tendons, which fibre type is relatively more prominent in many ligaments?
exp: Ligaments remain collagen-rich, but elastic fibres are relatively more prominent in many ligaments than in tendons.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which is more flexible: tendon or ligament?
exp: Tendon connects bone to muscle and contains white collagen filaments. It is strong but has limited flexibility.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which comparison between tendon and ligament is correct?
a: Tendon connects muscle to bone and is collagen-rich; ligament connects bone to bone and is generally more elastic.
exp: Remember the exam distinction: tendon = muscle-to-bone; ligament = bone-to-bone. Both are dense connective tissues rich in collagen.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which set lists major substances transported by blood?
a: Respiratory gases, nutrients, hormones and metabolic wastes
exp: Blood is a fluid connective tissue that transports gases, nutrients, chemical messengers and wastes and also contributes to defence and homeostasis.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What percentage of blood is plasma?
exp: Plasma is the fluid matrix of blood and forms about 55% of blood. Its composition is about 90% water, 8% protein and 2% minerals or ions.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Approximately what fraction of whole blood is formed elements in a typical adult?
exp: RBCs, WBCs and platelets together are called formed elements and make up roughly 45% of blood volume, mainly because RBCs are so numerous. Calling all of this 'cells' is imprecise because platelets are cell fragments.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: How is plasma described?
exp: Plasma is the fluid matrix of blood and forms about 55% of blood. Its composition is about 90% water, 8% protein and 2% minerals or ions.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Approximately what percentage of blood plasma is water?
exp: Plasma is predominantly water, approximately 90–92%, which serves as the solvent for proteins and many transported solutes.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Approximately what proportion of plasma consists of proteins?
exp: Plasma proteins such as albumin, globulins and fibrinogen collectively account for roughly 6–8% of plasma.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Besides water and proteins, what does plasma contain?
a: Electrolytes and dissolved nutrients, gases, hormones and wastes
exp: The remaining plasma fraction contains many solutes; reducing it to a fixed '2% minerals' is misleading.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Why do red blood cells appear red?
a: Because they contain haemoglobin, an iron-containing respiratory pigment.
exp: Haemoglobin contains haem groups with iron and gives RBCs their characteristic red colour while binding oxygen.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What is the shape of RBC?
exp: RBCs are biconcave red cells; their red colour is linked with an iron-containing pigment. They are formed in bone marrow and destroyed in the spleen.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Where are most red blood cells produced in an adult human?
exp: Erythropoiesis in adults occurs mainly in red bone marrow.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Where are aged red blood cells mainly removed from circulation?
a: Mainly by macrophages in the spleen and liver
exp: The spleen is a major site of removal of senescent RBCs, and the liver also contributes substantially. Therefore 'destroyed only in spleen' is too absolute.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Why is the spleen traditionally called the 'graveyard of RBCs' in exam books?
a: Because it is a major site where aged or damaged RBCs are removed by macrophages.
exp: The phrase is useful as an exam mnemonic, but the liver also removes old RBCs; the spleen is not the exclusive site.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which WBC types are included?
a: Neutrophil, Eosinophil, Basophil, Lymphocyte and Monocyte.
exp: The WBC types included are Neutrophil, Eosinophil, Basophil, Lymphocyte and Monocyte.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What is the main function of platelets?
exp: Platelets are the blood component associated with blood clotting.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What colour is lymph?
exp: Lymph is colourless and RBCs are absent from it.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which statement about normal lymph is correct?
a: RBCs are normally absent, while lymphocytes are prominent cellular components.
exp: Normal lymph is a clear tissue fluid rich in lymphocytes and ordinarily lacks red blood cells.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which pairing correctly gives the main adult site of RBC formation and major sites of aged-RBC removal?
a: Formation: red bone marrow; removal: mainly spleen and liver
exp: Adult erythropoiesis occurs chiefly in red marrow, whereas senescent RBCs are phagocytosed mainly in spleen and liver.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which statement correctly describes lymph?
a: Lymph is colourless and RBCs are absent.
exp: Lymph is colourless and RBCs are absent from it.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Where is adipose tissue commonly found and what is its major role?
a: Under the skin and around many organs; it stores fat and provides insulation and cushioning.
exp: Adipose connective tissue stores triglycerides, reduces heat loss and cushions organs. It occurs subcutaneously and around structures such as kidneys.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What is the function of adipose tissue?
a: Fat storage, shock absorption and insulation.
exp: Adipose tissue contains fat-storage cells and occurs below the skin, around organs and in bone marrow. Its functions include fat storage, shock absorption and insulation.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Where is areolar connective tissue commonly found?
a: Beneath epithelia and around blood vessels, nerves and organs
exp: Areolar tissue is a loose connective tissue widely distributed beneath epithelia and around vessels, nerves and organs.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What is a major function of areolar connective tissue?
a: Binding and packing tissues, supporting structures and aiding tissue repair
exp: Areolar tissue acts as packing and binding material and contains cells important in defence and repair.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which connective tissue stores fat?
exp: Connective tissue connects different organs and body parts. Its cells are embedded in an intercellular matrix, and the group includes fibrous, fluid, loose and skeletal connective tissues.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which connective tissue provides shock absorption and insulation?
exp: Connective tissue connects different organs and body parts. Its cells are embedded in an intercellular matrix, and the group includes fibrous, fluid, loose and skeletal connective tissues.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which loose connective tissue repairs and fills empty spaces?
exp: Connective tissue connects different organs and body parts. Its cells are embedded in an intercellular matrix, and the group includes fibrous, fluid, loose and skeletal connective tissues.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: How is the matrix of areolar tissue described?
exp: Areolar tissue has a loose jelly-like matrix and occurs below the skin, in spaces of hollow organs, and near muscles and blood vessels. It helps repair tissues and fill empty spaces.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which description of bone matrix is chemically accurate?
a: A collagen-rich organic matrix mineralised mainly with calcium phosphate as hydroxyapatite.
exp: Bone rigidity comes mainly from calcium-phosphate mineral, chiefly hydroxyapatite, deposited in a collagenous matrix. The formula 'CaPO4' is not a chemically valid way to name the bone mineral.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which cells are primarily responsible for forming new bone matrix?
exp: Osteoblasts synthesise the organic components of bone matrix and promote mineralisation. Bone provides support, protection and leverage for movement.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which description of cartilage is correct?
a: It is a firm but flexible connective tissue with chondrocytes in lacunae and a matrix rich in collagen; elastic cartilage also contains elastic fibres.
exp: Cartilage is less rigid than bone and its mature cells, chondrocytes, occupy lacunae. Collagen is a major matrix fibre; elastic fibres are especially abundant in elastic cartilage.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which set contains recognised locations of cartilage in the human body?
a: Articular surfaces of joints, nose, pinna and tracheal rings
exp: Cartilage supports flexible structures such as the nose and pinna, forms tracheal rings and covers many joint surfaces.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which inorganic material is the principal mineral component of bone?
a: Calcium phosphate, chiefly in hydroxyapatite crystals
exp: Hydroxyapatite, a calcium-phosphate mineral, is the dominant inorganic component responsible for much of bone's hardness.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What are osteoblasts?
exp: Bone is hard and stiff because its matrix contains calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate salts. Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells, and bone provides support, protection and body shape.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What are the major functions of bone?
exp: Bone is hard and stiff because its matrix contains calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate salts. Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells, and bone provides support, protection and body shape.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: What are the mature cells of cartilage called?
exp: Chondrocytes are mature cartilage cells and lie in spaces called lacunae. 'Chondrin' is an old, imprecise term for cartilage matrix and should not be treated as a specific key matrix protein.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which protein fibre is a major structural component of cartilage matrix?
exp: Collagen fibres are important components of cartilage matrix. Elastic cartilage additionally contains abundant elastic fibres.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Name five locations of cartilage
a: Joints, tip of nose, outer ear, trachea and throat.
exp: Cartilage is flexible and strong and is associated with chondrin, collagen and elastin fibres. It occurs at joints, the tip of the nose, outer ear, trachea and throat.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which is hard and stiff: bone or cartilage?
exp: Cartilage is flexible and strong and is associated with chondrin, collagen and elastin fibres. It occurs at joints, the tip of the nose, outer ear, trachea and throat.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which is flexible and strong: bone or cartilage?
exp: Cartilage is flexible and strong and is associated with chondrin, collagen and elastin fibres. It occurs at joints, the tip of the nose, outer ear, trachea and throat.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Which statement correctly compares bone and cartilage?
a: Bone is highly mineralised and rigid; cartilage is less mineralised and more flexible.
exp: Bone has a strongly mineralised collagen matrix; cartilage has a firm but comparatively flexible matrix with chondrocytes.

section: 6. Connective Tissue - Fibrous, Fluid, Loose & Skeletal
q: Where are haematopoietic stem cells chiefly found in an adult?
exp: Haematopoietic stem cells in red marrow give rise to the cellular lineages of blood. Saying simply 'stem cells are present in bone marrow' is too broad because many stem-cell types exist.

q: What type of cells are muscle fibres?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: How does muscular movement occur?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: Which two proteins are responsible for muscle contraction?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: Is striated / skeletal muscle branched or unbranched?
exp: Striated or skeletal muscle is unbranched, elongated and cylindrical, multinucleate, striated and voluntary. It is attached to the skeleton and fatigues relatively quickly.

q: What is the shape of striated / skeletal muscle?
exp: Striated or skeletal muscle is unbranched, elongated and cylindrical, multinucleate, striated and voluntary. It is attached to the skeleton and fatigues relatively quickly.

q: What is the nuclear condition of striated / skeletal muscle?
exp: Striated or skeletal muscle is unbranched, elongated and cylindrical, multinucleate, striated and voluntary. It is attached to the skeleton and fatigues relatively quickly.

q: What produces the striated appearance of skeletal muscle fibres?
a: Regular alternating light and dark transverse bands produced by the ordered myofilaments.
exp: Skeletal muscle is striated because actin and myosin are organised into repeating sarcomeres, producing alternating light and dark bands.

q: Which muscle tissue is normally under voluntary control?
exp: Skeletal muscle is controlled mainly by the somatic nervous system and is usually voluntary.

q: Which feature is NOT characteristic of skeletal muscle?
a: Branched fibres joined by intercalated discs
exp: Intercalated discs and branching are characteristic of cardiac muscle, not skeletal muscle. Skeletal fibres are long, cylindrical, striated and multinucleate.

q: Where is striated / skeletal muscle found?
exp: Striated or skeletal muscle is unbranched, elongated and cylindrical, multinucleate, striated and voluntary. It is attached to the skeleton and fatigues relatively quickly.

q: Is smooth / visceral muscle branched or unbranched?
exp: Smooth or visceral muscle is unbranched, elongated and spindle-shaped, uninucleate, unstriated and involuntary. It occurs in the walls of internal organs and is fatigue-resistant.

q: What is the shape of smooth / visceral muscle?
exp: Smooth or visceral muscle is unbranched, elongated and spindle-shaped, uninucleate, unstriated and involuntary. It occurs in the walls of internal organs and is fatigue-resistant.

q: What is the nuclear condition of smooth / visceral muscle?
exp: Smooth or visceral muscle is unbranched, elongated and spindle-shaped, uninucleate, unstriated and involuntary. It occurs in the walls of internal organs and is fatigue-resistant.

q: Which statement about smooth muscle is correct?
a: It lacks visible transverse striations under the light microscope.
exp: Smooth muscle contains actin and myosin but they are not organised into the regular sarcomeres that produce visible striations.

q: How is visceral smooth muscle mainly controlled?
a: Involuntarily through autonomic, hormonal and local mechanisms.
exp: Smooth muscle in visceral organs generally contracts involuntarily and is regulated by autonomic nerves, hormones and local factors.

q: Which functional pattern is typical of many smooth muscles?
a: Slow, sustained contractions with relatively high fatigue resistance.
exp: Many smooth muscles are adapted for tonic or sustained activity and are more fatigue-resistant than fast skeletal muscle fibres.

q: Where is smooth / visceral muscle found?
exp: Smooth or visceral muscle is unbranched, elongated and spindle-shaped, uninucleate, unstriated and involuntary. It occurs in the walls of internal organs and is fatigue-resistant.

q: Is cardiac muscle branched or unbranched?
exp: Cardiac muscle is branched, cylindrical and striated, but it is involuntary. It is uninucleate, contains intercalated discs and works lifelong without fatigue.

q: What is the shape of cardiac muscle?
exp: Cardiac muscle is branched, cylindrical and striated, but it is involuntary. It is uninucleate, contains intercalated discs and works lifelong without fatigue.

q: What is the usual nuclear condition of a human cardiac muscle cell?
a: Usually one centrally placed nucleus; some cells may have two.
exp: Cardiomyocytes are typically uninucleate with a central nucleus, although binucleate cells also occur.

q: Why does cardiac muscle appear striated?
a: Its actin and myosin are organised into sarcomeres.
exp: Like skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle has sarcomeres that create a striated microscopic appearance.

q: Is cardiac muscle voluntary or involuntary?
exp: Cardiac contractions are not under conscious voluntary control; heart rate and force are modulated by intrinsic pacemaking and autonomic/hormonal influences.

q: Which statement best describes the fatigue resistance of cardiac muscle?
a: It is highly fatigue-resistant under normal physiological conditions and is adapted for lifelong rhythmic activity.
exp: Cardiac muscle has abundant mitochondria, rich blood supply and aerobic metabolism, making it highly resistant to fatigue. 'No fatigue ever' is too absolute.

q: Where is cardiac muscle found?
exp: Cardiac muscle is branched, cylindrical and striated, but it is involuntary. It is uninucleate, contains intercalated discs and works lifelong without fatigue.

q: Which muscle is voluntary?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: Which muscles are involuntary?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: Which muscles show bands or striations?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: Which muscle has no striations?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: Which muscle is spindle-shaped?
exp: Smooth or visceral muscle is unbranched, elongated and spindle-shaped, uninucleate, unstriated and involuntary. It occurs in the walls of internal organs and is fatigue-resistant.

q: Which muscle is multinucleate?
exp: Striated or skeletal muscle is unbranched, elongated and cylindrical, multinucleate, striated and voluntary. It is attached to the skeleton and fatigues relatively quickly.

q: Which statement correctly compares nuclei in smooth and cardiac muscle cells?
a: Smooth muscle cells usually have one central nucleus; cardiac cells usually have one central nucleus but may occasionally have two.
exp: Both cell types are generally centrally nucleated; occasional binucleate cardiomyocytes are a recognised exception.

exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: In which muscle are intercalated discs present?
exp: Cardiac muscle is branched, cylindrical and striated, but it is involuntary. It is uninucleate, contains intercalated discs and works lifelong without fatigue.

q: Which muscle is specially adapted for continuous rhythmic activity and is highly fatigue-resistant?
exp: Cardiac muscle works continuously throughout life and has metabolic adaptations that confer very high fatigue resistance.

q: Which statement correctly describes cardiac-muscle?
exp: Cardiac muscle is branched, cylindrical and striated, but it is involuntary. It is uninucleate, contains intercalated discs and works lifelong without fatigue.

q: Which statement correctly describes smooth-muscle?
exp: Smooth or visceral muscle is unbranched, elongated and spindle-shaped, uninucleate, unstriated and involuntary. It occurs in the walls of internal organs and is fatigue-resistant.

q: Which statement correctly describes skeletal-muscle?
exp: Striated or skeletal muscle is unbranched, elongated and cylindrical, multinucleate, striated and voluntary. It is attached to the skeleton and fatigues relatively quickly.

q: What are the main functions of nervous tissue?
a: Sensitivity, excitability and coordination among organ systems.
exp: Nervous tissue provides sensitivity, excitability and coordination among organ systems. It occurs in the brain, spinal cord and nerves.

q: What is the structural and functional unit of nervous tissue?
exp: Nervous tissue provides sensitivity, excitability and coordination among organ systems. It occurs in the brain, spinal cord and nerves.

q: How long can the axon of a human neuron become?
a: Some axons can extend for more than one metre.
exp: Long motor and sensory neurons can have axons extending from the spinal cord to distal limbs, exceeding one metre in tall adults.

q: Which statement about division of mature neurons is most accurate?
a: Most mature neurons are terminally differentiated and generally do not undergo mitosis.
exp: For standard exam biology, mature neurons are considered post-mitotic. Avoid the absolute wording 'no neuron can ever be replaced', because limited neurogenesis and neural progenitor cells exist in specific contexts.

q: Where is nervous tissue found?
exp: Nervous tissue provides sensitivity, excitability and coordination among organ systems. It occurs in the brain, spinal cord and nerves.

q: What is the relation between Schwann cells and the neurilemma in peripheral nerves?
a: The outer Schwann-cell layer forms the neurilemma around many peripheral nerve fibres.
exp: Schwann cells are glial cells of the peripheral nervous system. Their outer nucleated cytoplasmic layer constitutes the neurilemma; calling Schwann cells simply 'neurilemma cells' obscures this relationship.

q: Which statement about nervous tissue is correct?
a: Most mature neurons are post-mitotic, while Schwann cells support peripheral nerve fibres and form neurilemma.
exp: This combines two high-yield facts without equating Schwann cells with neurilemma: mature neurons generally do not divide, and Schwann cells form/support the neurilemma in the PNS.

q: What is eosin in routine histological staining?
a: An acidic dye that stains many cytoplasmic and extracellular proteins pink to red.
exp: Eosin is the acidic counterstain in the common H&E method; eosinophilic proteins appear pink to red.

q: Which structures are commonly eosinophilic in H&E-stained sections?
a: Much of the cytoplasm, collagen and red blood cells
exp: Eosin binds many basic protein components, so cytoplasm, extracellular collagen and RBCs typically stain shades of pink or red.

q: Which type of stem cell is classically found in red bone marrow and gives rise to blood cells?
exp: Haematopoietic stem cells in red marrow generate erythroid, myeloid and lymphoid blood-cell lineages.

q: What is the colour of lymph?
exp: Lymph is colourless and RBCs are absent from it.

q: Which formed element of blood is normally absent from lymph?
exp: Normal lymph contains lymphocytes and may contain other leukocytes, but RBCs are ordinarily absent.

q: Tips of shoots and roots + elongation points to which meristem?
exp: Apical meristem occurs at the developing tips of roots and shoots and causes elongation. The key pairing is tip position with growth in length.

q: A meristem located at the bases of leaves or internodes in grasses and responsible for elongation/regrowth is:
exp: Intercalary meristem is retained between mature tissues, commonly at basal regions of leaves or internodes in grasses.

q: Sides of stems and roots + girth points to which meristem?
exp: Lateral meristem lies along the sides of stems and roots and is associated with secondary increase in thickness or girth.

q: Living + storage + thin wall + intercellular spaces points to which tissue?
exp: Parenchyma is a living simple permanent tissue with thin-walled isodiametric cells and intercellular spaces. It commonly stores food and water and occurs in cortex, pith and leaf mesophyll.

q: Living + corner thickening + flexible support points to which tissue?
exp: Collenchyma is a living simple permanent tissue with elongated cells and corner thickening of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin. It provides mechanical support with flexibility.

q: Dead + lignified thick wall + coconut husk points to which tissue?
exp: Sclerenchyma is dead at maturity and has elongated narrow cells with thick cellulose-and-lignin walls and no intercellular spaces. It provides strength and mechanical support and occurs in structures such as coconut husk, seed coat and leaf veins.

q: Parenchyma with chloroplasts points to what modification?
exp: Chlorenchyma is parenchyma containing chloroplasts, so its main role is photosynthesis. It is especially important in leaves and herbaceous stems.

q: Parenchyma with large air spaces points to what modification?
exp: Aerenchyma is parenchyma with large air spaces. These air spaces provide buoyancy, making it especially important in aquatic plants.

q: Aquatic buoyancy is a clue for which tissue modification?
exp: Aerenchyma is parenchyma with large air spaces. These air spaces provide buoyancy, making it especially important in aquatic plants.

q: Photosynthesis in a modified parenchyma points to which tissue?
exp: Chlorenchyma is parenchyma containing chloroplasts, so its main role is photosynthesis. It is especially important in leaves and herbaceous stems.

q: Predominantly upward transport of water and dissolved minerals from roots is a function of:
exp: Xylem conducts water and dissolved mineral ions mainly from roots toward aerial organs.

q: Source-to-sink translocation of organic assimilates, which may occur upward or downward, is a function of:
exp: Phloem distributes sucrose and other assimilates according to source–sink relationships.

q: Which is the only living component of xylem?
exp: Xylem is a complex permanent tissue that carries water and minerals mainly upward from roots through the stem to leaves. Its components include tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres; xylem parenchyma is the living component.

q: Dead cells + suberin + no intercellular spaces points to what protective tissue?
exp: Cork consists of multilayered thick dead cells arranged densely without intercellular spaces. Suberin deposited in the cell walls makes cork waterproof.

q: Outermost continuous single layer of a plant points to what tissue?
exp: Epidermis is the outermost continuous single protective layer of the plant, usually waxy. It may develop a waterproof cuticle, while root hairs increase the surface area for water absorption.

q: Waterproof waxy cuticle in desert plants is associated with what tissue?
exp: Epidermis is the outermost continuous single protective layer of the plant, usually waxy. It may develop a waterproof cuticle, while root hairs increase the surface area for water absorption.

q: Kidney- or bean-shaped guard cells are common in:
exp: Many dicots have kidney/bean-shaped guard cells, whereas grasses characteristically have dumbbell-shaped guard cells.

q: Dumbbell-shaped guard cells are characteristic of:
exp: Grasses are the standard textbook example of dumbbell-shaped guard cells; this should not be generalised to all monocots.

q: Turgid guard cells indicate what condition of stomata?
exp: Stomata are small pores on the leaf epidermis that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Turgid guard cells open the pore, while water loss makes guard cells relaxed or shrunken and closes it.

q: Shrunken / relaxed guard cells indicate what condition of stomata?
exp: Stomata are small pores on the leaf epidermis that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Turgid guard cells open the pore, while water loss makes guard cells relaxed or shrunken and closes it.

q: Thin flat single-layer epithelium in alveoli points to what type?
exp: Simple squamous epithelium is a thin, flat, single layer. It is found in blood vessels, alveoli, the mouth and alimentary canal.

q: Multilayered epithelium of skin points to what type?
exp: Stratified squamous epithelium is multilayered and is the epithelial type associated with skin.

q: Cube-shaped epithelium in kidney tubules points to what type?
exp: Cuboidal epithelium is made of cube-shaped cells. It is associated with kidney tubules, sweat glands, salivary glands and thyroid glands.

q: Column-shaped epithelium in stomach and intestine points to what type?
exp: Columnar epithelium has column-shaped cells and is associated with the stomach, intestine, gall bladder and bile duct.

q: Epithelium with motile cilia in the trachea and oviduct is:
exp: Ciliated columnar epithelium helps move mucus in respiratory passages and assists movement of the ovum/early embryo in the oviduct.

q: Goblet cell points to what epithelial category?
exp: A goblet cell represents single-cell glandular epithelium, while glands are the multicellular form. Salivary and thyroid glands are the examples paired with the multicellular form.

q: Bone-to-muscle + white collagen points to what connective tissue?
exp: Bone is hard and stiff because its matrix contains calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate salts. Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells, and bone provides support, protection and body shape.

q: A dense connective tissue that connects bone to bone and is generally more elastic than tendon is:
exp: Ligaments connect bones at joints. They are collagen-rich and commonly contain relatively more elastic fibres than tendons.

q: 55% of blood points to which component?
exp: Blood is a connective tissue that transports nutrients, oxygen/carbon dioxide, hormones and excretory materials. About 55% is plasma and 45% is cells.

q: A biconcave blood cell produced chiefly in red bone marrow and removed when aged mainly in spleen/liver is:
exp: Mature human RBCs are biconcave, arise by erythropoiesis in red marrow, and senescent cells are cleared mainly by macrophages of spleen and liver.

q: Blood clotting points to which blood component?
exp: Platelets are the blood component associated with blood clotting.

q: Colourless fluid with no RBC points to what?
exp: RBCs are biconcave red cells; their red colour is linked with an iron-containing pigment. They are formed in bone marrow and destroyed in the spleen.

q: Fat storage + insulation + shock absorption points to what tissue?
exp: Adipose tissue contains fat-storage cells and occurs below the skin, around organs and in bone marrow. Its functions include fat storage, shock absorption and insulation.

q: Loose jelly-like matrix + repair and filling spaces points to what tissue?
exp: Areolar tissue has a loose jelly-like matrix and occurs below the skin, in spaces of hollow organs, and near muscles and blood vessels. It helps repair tissues and fill empty spaces.

q: A collagenous matrix mineralised mainly with calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite), with osteoblasts forming matrix, identifies:
exp: Bone combines a collagen-rich organic matrix with hydroxyapatite mineral; osteoblasts form new bone matrix.

q: Firm but flexible connective tissue containing chondrocytes in lacunae is:
exp: Cartilage is characterised by chondrocytes embedded in a firm, flexible extracellular matrix.

q: Actin + myosin points to which broad tissue?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: Voluntary + multinucleate + striations points to what muscle?
exp: Striated or skeletal muscle is unbranched, elongated and cylindrical, multinucleate, striated and voluntary. It is attached to the skeleton and fatigues relatively quickly.

q: Spindle-shaped + uninucleate + no striations points to what muscle?
exp: Smooth or visceral muscle is unbranched, elongated and spindle-shaped, uninucleate, unstriated and involuntary. It occurs in the walls of internal organs and is fatigue-resistant.

q: Branched + striated + involuntary + intercalated discs points to what muscle?
exp: Cardiac muscle is branched, cylindrical and striated, but it is involuntary. It is uninucleate, contains intercalated discs and works lifelong without fatigue.

q: Which muscle is highly fatigue-resistant and adapted for lifelong rhythmic contractions?
exp: Cardiac muscle is highly fatigue-resistant under normal physiology; 'never fatigues under any condition' is an overstatement.

q: Structural and functional unit of nervous tissue points to what cell?
exp: Nervous tissue provides sensitivity, excitability and coordination among organ systems. It occurs in the brain, spinal cord and nerves.

q: A highly specialised excitable cell that may have an axon longer than one metre and is generally post-mitotic when mature is a:
exp: Neurons are excitable cells specialised for signal transmission; most mature neurons do not normally undergo mitosis.

q: In a myelinated peripheral nerve fibre, the neurilemma is formed by:
a: The outer nucleated cytoplasmic layer of the Schwann cell
exp: Schwann cells ensheath peripheral axons; their outer cytoplasmic layer constitutes the neurilemma.

q: An acidic dye used in H&E staining that colours many cytoplasmic proteins pink-red is:
exp: Eosin is the acidic counterstain of H&E and commonly stains cytoplasm, collagen and RBCs pink to red.

q: Robert Hooke's observation of box-like compartments in cork led to the introduction of the term:
exp: Hooke used the term 'cells' for the compartments he saw in cork.

q: Tissue is best defined as:
a: An organised group of similar cells, with intercellular substance where present, performing a specific function.
exp: Tissue organisation enables division of labour between groups of specialised cells.

q: Plant tissue broad groups?
exp: Plant tissues are broadly divided into meristematic tissue and permanent tissue. Meristematic tissue retains dividing capacity, whereas permanent tissue is differentiated and lacks active division.

q: Animal tissue four types?
exp: Animal tissue is divided into four major types: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous. Their primary roles are protection/lining, connection, movement and sensitivity/coordination respectively; animal tissues are mostly living.

q: Apical meristem function?

q: Intercalary meristem location?
exp: Intercalary meristem occurs at leaf bases and at nodes or internodes, where it contributes to length growth of stems and leaves.

q: Intercalary meristem function?
exp: Intercalary meristem occurs at leaf bases and at nodes or internodes, where it contributes to length growth of stems and leaves.

exp: Lateral meristem lies along the sides of stems and roots and is associated with secondary increase in thickness or girth.

q: A typical meristematic cell has:
a: No large central vacuole; vacuoles are absent or very small.
exp: Actively dividing meristematic cells have dense cytoplasm and lack the prominent central vacuole of many mature plant cells.

q: Intercellular spaces in meristematic tissue are generally:
exp: Meristematic cells are compactly arranged, so conspicuous intercellular spaces are absent.

q: Aerenchyma?
a: Parenchyma with large air spaces - aquatic buoyancy.

q: Xylem chiefly transports:
a: Water and dissolved minerals, predominantly from roots upward.
exp: Xylem is the main long-distance water- and mineral-conducting tissue in vascular plants.

q: Living xylem component?
exp: Xylem is a complex permanent tissue that carries water and minerals mainly upward from roots through the stem to leaves. Its components include tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres; xylem parenchyma is the living component.

q: Phloem chiefly transports:
a: Organic assimilates from sources to sinks; direction may be upward or downward.
exp: Phloem translocation follows source–sink relationships rather than a fixed single direction.

q: Protective plant tissues?
exp: The two protective plant tissues are epidermis and cork. Epidermis forms the outer protective layer, while cork consists of dead, densely arranged cells whose suberin makes it waterproof.

q: Cork waterproof substance?
exp: Cork consists of multilayered thick dead cells arranged densely without intercellular spaces. Suberin deposited in the cell walls makes cork waterproof.

q: Cork cells?
a: Dead; densely arranged; no intercellular spaces.

q: Stomata function?
exp: Stomata are small pores on the leaf epidermis that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Turgid guard cells open the pore, while water loss makes guard cells relaxed or shrunken and closes it.

q: Guard cells are commonly kidney/bean-shaped in:
exp: Many dicots show kidney/bean-shaped guard cells.

q: Guard cells are characteristically dumbbell-shaped in:

q: Stoma opens when?
a: Guard cells become turgid as water enters.

q: Skin epithelium?
exp: Stratified squamous epithelium is multilayered and is the epithelial type associated with skin.

q: Kidney tubule epithelium?
exp: Cuboidal epithelium is made of cube-shaped cells. It is associated with kidney tubules, sweat glands, salivary glands and thyroid glands.

q: Trachea epithelium?
exp: Ciliated columnar epithelium bears motile cilia on its free surface. Standard examples include respiratory passages such as the trachea and the oviduct; the cilia move mucus or reproductive material along the surface.

q: Stomach / intestine epithelium?
exp: Columnar epithelium has column-shaped cells and is associated with the stomach, intestine, gall bladder and bile duct.

q: Alveoli epithelium?
exp: Simple squamous epithelium is a thin, flat, single layer. It is found in blood vessels, alveoli, the mouth and alimentary canal.

q: Goblet cell tissue?
exp: A goblet cell represents single-cell glandular epithelium, while glands are the multicellular form. Salivary and thyroid glands are the examples paired with the multicellular form.

q: Tendon connects:
a: Muscle to bone; it is rich in collagen fibres.
exp: Tendons are collagen-rich dense connective tissues transmitting muscle force to bone.

q: Ligament connects:
a: Bone to bone; it is collagen-rich and generally more elastic than tendon.
exp: Ligaments stabilise joints by connecting bones and are generally more elastic than tendons, while still being collagen-rich.

q: What percentage of blood is plasma?
exp: Plasma is the fluid matrix of blood and forms about 55% of blood. Its composition is about 90% water, 8% protein and 2% minerals or ions.

q: Formed elements make up approximately what percentage of whole blood?
exp: RBCs, WBCs and platelets collectively constitute roughly 45% of blood volume; plasma makes up roughly 55%.

q: Which description of plasma composition is most accurate?
a: About 90–92% water, about 6–8% proteins, plus electrolytes and other dissolved solutes.
exp: Plasma contains a range of dissolved substances in addition to water and proteins, so a rigid '2% minerals only' remainder is inaccurate.

q: Most RBCs in an adult human are formed in:
exp: Red bone marrow is the principal site of adult erythropoiesis.

q: Aged RBCs are removed mainly by macrophages in:
exp: The spleen is classically called the 'graveyard of RBCs', but the liver also plays an important role in removing senescent RBCs.

q: RBC shape?
exp: RBCs are biconcave red cells; their red colour is linked with an iron-containing pigment. They are formed in bone marrow and destroyed in the spleen.

q: WBC types?
exp: The WBC types included are Neutrophil, Eosinophil, Basophil, Lymphocyte and Monocyte.

q: Platelets function?
exp: Platelets are the blood component associated with blood clotting.

q: Lymph colour / RBC?
exp: Lymph is colourless and RBCs are absent from it.

q: Adipose main role?
exp: Adipose tissue contains fat-storage cells and occurs below the skin, around organs and in bone marrow. Its functions include fat storage, shock absorption and insulation.

q: Areolar function?
exp: Areolar tissue has a loose jelly-like matrix and occurs below the skin, in spaces of hollow organs, and near muscles and blood vessels. It helps repair tissues and fill empty spaces.

q: The principal mineral in bone matrix is:
exp: Bone mineral is dominated by hydroxyapatite, a calcium-phosphate mineral; 'CaPO4' should not be used as the formula.

q: Bone-forming cells?
exp: Bone is hard and stiff because its matrix contains calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate salts. Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells, and bone provides support, protection and body shape.

q: The mature cell of cartilage is called:
exp: Chondrocytes occupy lacunae in cartilage matrix. 'Chondrin' is not an appropriate modern answer to a question asking for a key matrix protein.

q: Which set lists common cartilage locations?
a: Joint surfaces, nose, pinna and tracheal rings
exp: Cartilage supports flexible structures and reduces friction at many joints.

q: Muscle contractile proteins?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: Voluntary muscle?
exp: Muscle fibres are elongated contractile cells. Movement occurs through contraction and relaxation, and actin and myosin are the contractile proteins involved.

q: Intercalated discs?
exp: Cardiac muscle is branched, cylindrical and striated, but it is involuntary. It is uninucleate, contains intercalated discs and works lifelong without fatigue.

q: Cardiac muscle control?
exp: Cardiac muscle is branched, cylindrical and striated, but it is involuntary. It is uninucleate, contains intercalated discs and works lifelong without fatigue.

q: Cardiac muscle is best described as:
a: Highly fatigue-resistant and adapted for continuous rhythmic activity.
exp: Cardiac muscle is designed for lifelong rhythmic contraction and is extremely fatigue-resistant under normal conditions.

q: Neuron?
a: Structural and functional unit of nervous tissue.
exp: Neuron is the structural and functional unit of nervous tissue. A neuron may reach about 1 m in length and does not have dividing capability.

q: Most mature neurons are:
a: Post-mitotic and generally do not divide by mitosis.
exp: For exam purposes, mature neurons are generally considered non-dividing/post-mitotic; avoid absolute claims that ignore limited neurogenesis in specialised settings.

q: Some human neuronal axons can reach:
a: More than one metre in length
exp: Axons of neurons extending to distal limbs can exceed one metre in tall adults.

q: Neurilemma of many peripheral nerve fibres is formed by:
a: The outer nucleated cytoplasm of Schwann cells
exp: Schwann cells form the neurilemma; the two terms should not be treated as simple synonyms.

q: Eosin is:
a: An acidic dye that stains many cytoplasmic/extracellular proteins and RBCs pink-red.
exp: Eosin is the acidic counterstain used with haematoxylin in H&E staining.

q: Haematopoietic stem cells in adults are found chiefly in:
exp: Red bone marrow houses haematopoietic stem cells that generate the formed cellular lineages of blood.
